hints: Split the ester at the single C-O bond next to the C=O group and look at the two sides separately to find the acid part and the alcohol part.
walkthrough:
Split the ester into its two parent parts**
Picture the central $\text{COO}$ group. The side that includes the $\text{C=O}$ carbon comes from the carboxylic acid, here it is $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}$, which is a 2 carbon ethanoate part. The side attached through the O atom comes from the alcohol, here it is a 3 carbon straight chain, a propyl group.

hints: Remember the difference between acid hydrolysis which gives carboxylic acid plus alcohol, and alkaline hydrolysis which gives carboxylate salt plus alcohol.
walkthrough:
Link salt formation to alkaline hydrolysis**
An ester plus water with acid catalyst gives a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. To get the salt of the acid instead, you need an alkali to neutralise the acid as it forms. Warming with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ therefore gives sodium ethanoate plus propan-1-ol.

hints: Look at the O-alkyl side of ester V in (a)(i) and count how many carbons belong to the alcohol that is released on hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Recover the alcohol from the O-alkyl group**
The $\text{OCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ part of V becomes $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ after hydrolysis. That is propan-1-ol with the OH on carbon 1. In a displayed formula you draw every atom and every bond: three carbons in a chain, each with its H atoms shown, plus a $\text{C}-\text{O}-\text{H}$ ending.

Final answer: Displayed formula of propan-1-ol: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ shown with all bonds, $\text{C}-\text{H}$, $\text{C}-\text{C}$, $\text{C}-\text{O}$ and $\text{O}-\text{H}$ displayed.

hints: Think about the pleasant sweet smell of esters and their ability to dissolve other organic substances.
walkthrough:
Recall why esters are useful beyond flavour**
Esters are volatile liquids with sweet fruity smells and they are good solvents for organic compounds. So apart from food flavouring they are widely used in perfumes, cosmetics, inks, glues and as solvents.

hints: Treat the percentages as masses in 100 g, so you have 54.5 g of C, 9.1 g of H and 36.4 g of O to convert to moles.
Divide each percentage by the relevant $A_r$ ($\text{C}=12.0$, $\text{H}=1.0$, $\text{O}=16.0$) to get the moles of each element.
Divide all three mole values by the smallest one to get the simplest ratio, then round to whole numbers for the empirical formula.
walkthrough:
Convert percent to moles**
Imagine 100 g of W. Then $$n = \frac{mass}{A_r}$$ So $$n(\text{C}) = \frac{54.5}{12.0} = 4.54$$ $$n(\text{H}) = \frac{9.1}{1.0} = 9.1$$ $$n(\text{O}) = \frac{36.4}{16.0} = 2.275$$

Divide by the smallest to get the ratio**
The smallest is 2.275 for O. $$\text{C}: \frac{4.54}{2.275} = 1.99 \approx 2$$ $$\text{H}: \frac{9.1}{2.275} = 4.0$$ $$\text{O}: \frac{2.275}{2.275} = 1$$

Write the simplest whole number formula**
The ratio $\text{C}:\text{H}:\text{O} = 2:4:1$ gives the empirical formula $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}$. This is the simplest ratio, not necessarily the actual number of atoms in the molecule.

hints: Think about what links the empirical formula mass to the true molecular mass and how you would find that link.
walkthrough:
See why empirical is not enough**
The empirical formula only gives the ratio. Multiples like $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}$, $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{2}$ all share the same ratio. If you know the $M_r$, you can work out which multiple is the true molecular formula.
Final answer: relative molecular mass / $M_r$ of W

hints: Count carbons, hydrogens and oxygens carefully in any one of X, Y or Z, remembering that line ends and junctions represent carbon atoms with enough hydrogens to make four bonds.
walkthrough:
Count atoms in the skeletal structures**
Take Y, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$: that is 3 carbons, 6 hydrogens and 2 oxygens. X, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OCHO}$, and Z, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOCH}_{3}$, both count to the same total. So all three share molecular formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2}$.

hints: Recall which functional group contains an acidic O-H proton that can react with Na to release hydrogen gas.
Compare Y which has a $\text{COOH}$ group with X and Z which are esters with no O-H bond.
walkthrough:
Spot the only acidic proton**
Sodium metal reacts with labile protons in $\text{O}-\text{H}$ groups to give hydrogen gas: $$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_{2}$$ Carboxylic acids react readily like this. Esters have no $\text{O}-\text{H}$ proton, so they do not react.

Assign the observations**
Y is propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, so you see effervescence as $\text{H}_{2}$ bubbles off. X (ethyl methanoate) and Z (methyl ethanoate) are both esters, so no visible change with Na, ignoring any temperature change.
Final answer: Na + X: no reaction / no visible change\nNa + Y: effervescence / bubbles of gas\nNa + Z: no reaction / no visible change

hints: Remember the general pattern for any acid plus carbonate: salt plus carbon dioxide plus water, then apply it to methanoic acid and sodium carbonate.
walkthrough:
Build and balance the carbonate equation**
Methanoic acid, $\text{HCOOH}$ or $\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H}$, neutralises sodium carbonate to give sodium methanoate. You need two acids to provide two $\text{H}^{+}$ for one $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ to make $\text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Balanced: $$2\text{HCO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} \rightarrow 2\text{HCO}_{2}\text{Na} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
